html:
The Chipko movement was a forest protest in the Himalaya of what is now Uttarakhand, India, that began in 1973. Villagers hugged trees to stop contractors from cutting them; chipko means to cling.

Hill villages depended on the forests for fuel, fodder and water, but the government sold felling rights to outside companies. Activists led by Chandi Prasad Bhatt stopped a sports goods firm from cutting ash trees near Gopeshwar in 1973. In 1974 at Reni, Gaura Devi and the village women held off loggers while the men were away. The tactic recalled the Bishnoi of Rajasthan, who died in 1730 to save their trees.

The movement used the nonviolent methods of Mahatma Gandhi. Sunderlal Bahuguna walked across the hills to spread it. In 1980 Indira Gandhi banned green felling in the Uttarakhand Himalaya for fifteen years. Chipko became a model for the environmental movement worldwide, and an early example of women leading one.
